 ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Import of Coaches 
*81. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have imported rail coaches from Germany; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and the justification thereof; 
(c) whether import of coaches from foreign countries and the terms and 
conditions for such imports have been widely criticised; 
(d) whether indigenous coach manufacturing industry has been affected 
adversely due to import of such coaches; and 
(e) if so, the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUMAR): (a) to (e) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) At present, coaches being manufactured in India are of a technology 
of 1950's and need improvements as regards reduction in tare weight, reduction 
in maintenance and operation costs, resistance to corrosion, sealing capacity, 
safety features, speed potential, braking system, riding and passenger comforts, 
availability and reliability, etc. Therefore, country needed new design of coaches 
so that alongwith improved safely and Comfort, more number of passengers 
could be carried per coach/train and the maintenance and operation costs could 
be reduced, so as to be cost effective in the long run for Indian Railways. 
1 
 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001] 
In order to achieve the above objectives, it was decided to upgrade the design 
and manufacturing capabilities of Indian Railways by going in for procurement 
and transfer of technology of Light Weight Coaches of state-of-the-art technology 
with such features. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d)No, Sir. 
(e) Does not arise.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
The ten year Average Compound Growth Rate of agricultural Gross 
Domestic Product (GDP) ending 1999-2000 was 3.1 % per annum. To increase it to 
4% per annum, additional investment bot h by private sector and Government 
sector would be needed. According to the Quick Estimates of National Income 
for the year 1999-2000 released by the Central Statistical Organisation, the Gross 
Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) in Agriculture from Government sector was 
0.46% of the Gross Domestic Product, at 1993-94 prices. The GFCF of public 
sector in agriculture mainly consists of investment in irrigation projects. 
Allocation of public investment in agriculture will be known after the finalisation 
of the Tenth Plan. During the current year's budget substantial allocations have 
been provided for strengthening the infrastructure for the development of 
agriculture. These include additional flows of credit to agricultural sector (Rs. 
10,500 crore), additional funds for construction of roads under Pradhan 
Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (Rs. 2,500 crore) and enhanced allocations for rural 
electrification (Rs. 750crore), etc. All these will help in enhancing the investment 
in agriculture and consequently increase the rate of growth of agriculture.

been introduced in major cities.

research in the institution and particularly in its area of specialisation.

areas which arc relevant and useful to various development sectors

(iv) Institutions should have the n ecessary viability and a management 
capable of contributing to the university ideals and traditions. 
Ordinarily, institutions affiliated to universities and which are offering

M.Com./MSc, will not be considered for grant deemed to be university 
status. However, such institution wh ich is also offering innovative

recognition as a university. Supplementary assistance for innovation may be 
considered by the UGC only in such exceptional cases.

THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI NITISH KUM AR):(a) to (c) On 
22.6.2001 while 6602 Mangalore-Madras Mail was passing through Kadalundi 
station, 10 coaches derailed on the Kadalundi Bridge out of which five fell into the 
river, while some coaches were partially in water two were fully submerged in the 
river. The accident occured in Palghat Division of Southern Railway. 52 
passengers lost their lives and 314 received injuries as a result of this accident. 
Compensation claims for train accidents arc decided by Railway Claims 
Tribunal. No claim has been filed so far. Compensation shall be paid soon after the 
claim cases are decreed by the Railway Claims Tribunal, Ernakulam which has 
jurisdiction over the place of accident. However, ex-gratia announced by Minister 
for Railways amounting to Rs. 92.47 lakhs has been paid to next of kin of 
deceased and injured passengers so far. 
Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, who functions under the control of 
Ministry of Civil Aviation, has taken up statutory inquiry into this accident. His 
Final Report into the cause of the accident is awaited. 
(d) There arc 8713 rail bridges in Southern Railway which arc more than 100 
years old, 586 of these are major bridges. 
(e) There is an elaborate system of inspection and maintenance of bridges. 
These inspections are (a) Routine inspections (b) Special inspections carried out 
at various levels. The bridges arc thoroughly inspected by Assistant Engineers 
after the monsoon every year and details  observations are r ecorded in Bridge 
Inspection Registers. Instructions arc given for carrying out repairs of defects 
noticed during these inspections. Bridge Registers are sent for scrutiny and directions 
of Divisional Engineers and further to Chief Engineers. Based on observations in 
the registers, bridges requiring inspection at higher level are again inspected by 
Divisional Engineers and the Chief Engineers and the remedial actions are taken 
where required. 
For major bridges, the steel work and bearings arc inspected by the 
Assistant Bridge Engineers. These inspections arc recorded in the registers for 
inspection for steel works and bridges and Rivet Testing Register etc. The 
registers are then forwarded to the Deputy Chief Engineer (Bridges) and the 
Chief Bridge Engineers for their scru tiny and Directions. Urgent repairs are 
immediately carried out and planning done for major works of 
strengthening/rehabilitation & reconstruction, duly imposing suitable 
restrictions, as required.

Clearance to Pak table-tennis team 
* 95. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that delay in clearance has discouraged the 
Pakistan table-tennis team to participate in the 15th Commonwealth Table-
Tennis Championship; 
(b) if so, the reasons for delay in conveying the clearance; and 
(c) what steps have been taken to counter Pakistan media's contention 
of linking the delay to India's pulling out of Sharjah cricket tournament? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SUSHREE 
UMA BHARTI): (a) to (c) The Table- Tennis Federation of India (TTFI) 
submitted an application on 31.1.2001 seeking approval and financial 
assistance of Government for holding the 15th Commonwealth Table-Tennis 
Championship at New Delhi from 14th to 20th April, 2001. Thereafter, on 
13.2.2001, the Federation indicated that Pakistan and Fiji are not participating 
in this Championship. Accordingly, after obtaining the clearance of Ministry 
of External Affairs and Ministry of Home Affairs, permission was given to 
TTFI for holding the even' from 14th to 20th April, 2001. Later on, the Table-
Tennis Federation informed on 22.3.2001 that Pakistan has confirmed its 
participation. As such after obtaining the clearance of Ministry of External 
Affairs, the approval for inviting the Table-Tennis Team of Pakistan was 
conveyed on 11th April, 2001. As such, it will be seen that there has been no 
delay on the part of the Government of India in giving clearance to the 
participation of Pakistan Table-Tennis Team in the 15th Commonwealth Table-
Tennis Championship. 
There is no basis for linking Pakistan's non-participation in the 15th 
Commonwealth Table-Tennis Championship with India's decision not to play in 
Sharjah. India's decision for not playing in Sharjah Cricket tournament is based 
on a policy decision taken by the Government of India not to play any cricket 
matches at non-regular Cricket venues at least for a period of three years.

Benefits to Farmers from WTO and economic reforms 
t638. DR. MAHESH CHANDRA SHARMA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state the details of benefits likely to be derived 
by the common farmers of India, whose population is supposed to be around 78 
per cent, from World Trade Organisation and the so called liberal regulated 
economic reforms? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): World Trade Organisation (WTO) 
provides a predictable rule based multilateral trading system which protects the 
developing countries from the bilateral pressures of the developed trading 
partners. Being a fully democratic organisation, with equal voting rights to each 
member, India is assured of a say in the multilateral rule making process. 
WTO also has a strong Dispute Settlement Mechanism to resolve any disputes 
between members. By virtue of being a member of WTO, India is automatically 
entitled to get the most favoured nation (MFN) and national treatment from all 
other members for its exports. Farmers of India can have access to 
international market for exporting their crops and thereby can have the 
opportunity to get better prices for their products.

640. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government plan to subsidise export of farm 
products and remove Quantitative Restrictions (QR), to help farmers to export 
their products; 
(b) whether it is reported that additional steps have also been taken, such 
as providing credit at lower interest rates, etc; and 
(c) if so, what are the details of this plan and the result expected? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (c) Policy of exports of agricultural products 
forms an integral part of the Export/Import Policy of the country. The Policy 
regarding exports of agricultural products is governed principally by the concerns 
of India's food security, maximising farm incomes and earning foreign exchange. 
Review of export performance of agricultural products is an on-going process, 
and accordingly, policy interventions arc made, as and when considered 
necessary, with a view to making agricultural exports increasingly viable. Some 
of the steps taken/proposed to be taken are as follows:

of farmers.

quality control and modernization of processing units. 
• Arranging promotional campaigns such as buyer-seller meets and 
participation in important fairs and exhibitions.

market information.

to ensure quality, eliminating contamination and ensuring freedom from 
fungi and bacteria.

Food Security 
641. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to stale: 
(a) whether is a fact that India is more malnourished today than it was in 
1947; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the per capita availability of pulses has 
declined sharply from 78 gram per day at the time of independence to 40 gram 
per day at present; 
(c) whether the question of food security was discussed in national 
symposium held in the capital from 17lh to 19th April, 2001; and 
(d) if so, what are the details of the decisions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) It is not correct to say that India is more 
malnourished today than it was in 1947. At the time of independence clinical 
manifestations of various nutritional deficiencies like Beri Beri, Pellagra, 
Keratomalacia, Kwashiorkor and marasmus were widely prevalent. The near 
total disappearance of florid nutritional deficiency disorders, which were once 
major public health problems in India, has been remarkable experience. 
(b) The per capita availability of pulses has declined from 60.7 gms/day 
in 1951 to 32.0 gms/day in 2000. 
(c) A National Consultation on "Towards Hunger Free India" was jointly 
organized by the Planning Commission, the World Food Programme and MS 
Swaminathan Research Foundation in New Delhi between 24—26th April, 
2001. The discussion during the consultation revolved around the question of 
ensuring food security to all in India. 
(d) The National Consultation was held mainly to ascertain the views of 
experts on the question of food security. The different technical sessions as part 
of the Consultation deliberated upon the themes of (i) food availability and 
vulnerability to national disasters (ii) food absorption and utilization and (iii) 
sustainable livelihood and economic access to food.

Chief Minister's conference on impact of WTO agreement 
648.   SHRI V.V.RAGHAVAN: 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased so state: 
(a) whether a conference of Chief Ministers was held in Delhi to discuss 
the catastrophic impact of World Trade Organisation (WTO) agreement of Indian 
agriculture and farmers; and 
(b) if so, the details of discussion that took place and the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Department of Agriculture 
and Cooperation organized a Conference of Chief Ministers under the 
Chairmanship of Prime Minister on 21 st May, 2001 at New Delhi to discuss 
issues relating to the WTO Agreement on Agriculture and Food Management. 
The Chief Minister of 12 States and Union Ministers of Agriculture, Finance, 
Commerce and Industries, Food, Consumer Affairs and Public Distribution and 
Deputy Chairman (Planning Commission)  participated in the Conference, 
besides representatives of other States and Union Ministries. 
Discussion were held on the following agenda items: 
—  Agriculture Production Strategies: Diversification, post-harvest 
interventions 'Mid value addition, 
—  Removal of restrictions on movement and stocking of food and 
agricultural produce, 
—  Operation of the Essential Commodity Act, 1955 as applied to food 
and agricultural produce, 
—  Decentralisation of procurement and distribution, 
—  Impact of WTO on Indian Agriculture. 
The Conference provided an opportunity for a frank exchange of views 
and sharing of concerns and suggestions. The Prime Minister, during his 
concluding remarks, called for awareness building measures in order to remove 
misconceptions relating to WTO. He announced the constitution of a Standing 
Committee of Union Ministers and Chief Ministers to consider issues concerning 
agricultural strategics, food management and promotion of agricultural exports 
in the wake of WTO Agreement on Agriculture. 
70 

[27 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The first meeting for the Standing Committee on the Union Ministers 
and Chief Ministers on Food Management and Agricultural Exports was held 
on 6th July, 2001, where the following agenda items were discussed:— 
(i) Enhancing the efficiency of procurement and reducing the cost of 
distribution of foodgrains under PDS through decentralized and 
active involvement of the State. 
(ii) Implementation of the Food for Work Programme and Grain Bank 
Scheme. 
(iii) Review of Essential Commodities Act and Control Orders to ensure 
free movement. 
An Inter-Ministerial Group has been constituted by the Standing 
Committee to work out modalities of Food for Work Programme and Grain 
Bank Scheme. The Group is expected to submit its report in four weeks. On 
restructuring of the system of procurement of foodgrains, it was decided that 
the Government of India would work out a detailed proposal in consultation 
with the States. There was general consensus that the restrictions on movement 
of foodgrains need to be removed and that controls on trade of foodgrains need 
to be reviewed. 
With regard to building of awareness on WTO related issues, a series of 
State-level meetings are planned, two of which have already been held.

Cleaning of Yamuna 
663. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the status report proposed by the 
DDA, Urban Art Commission and other Government agencies on cleaning the 
Yamuna river; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the details of reports/project reports already proposed on cleaning the 
Yamuna river; and 
(d) the achievement made in cleaning the Yamuna so far and the Central 
assistance provided and utilized in this regard? 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Government is not aware of any status report prepared by 
the DDA or Urban Art Commission on cleaning of Yamuna river. However, the 
Government of National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi had commissioned a 
study to Water and Power Consultancy Services (WAPCOS) for preparation of a 
pre-feasibility report for construction of a parallel intercepting sewer along 
Yamuna in Delhi to prevent the discharge of untreated sewage into the river. A 
quick study report with an estimated cost of Rs. 800 crore was submitted by 
WAPCOS. The project was not found feasible as it envisaged to tackle only the 
point sources of pollution entering the river whereas as integrated action plan 
tackling all components responsible for pollution of Yamuna in Delhi is 
necessary for abatement of pollution in the river. 
(c) and(d) Government launched the Yamuna Action Plan in April, 1993 
for cleaning the river. The estimated cost  of the Action Plan is Rs. 510 crore 
comprising Rs. 226 crore for Haryana, Rs. 250 crore for Uttar Pradesh, Rs. 20 
crore for Delhi and the remaining Rs. 14 crore for miscellaneous items of work. 
In addition, under the extended phase of Yamuna Action Plan, a project at an 
estimated cost of Rs. 222 crore has been approved recently. The break up of the 
approved cost is: Haryana Rs. 22 crore, Delhi Rs. 167 crore, U.R Rs. 29 crore 
and the remaining Rs. 4 crore for miscellaneous works. The action plan covers 
21 towns of which 12 are in Haryana and 8 in Uttar Pradesh besides Delhi. All 
these works are targeted to be completed by March, 2002. In addition, the 
Government of NCT of Delhi is implementing projects for construction of 
additional sewage treatment plants, sewering of regularised unauthorised 
colonies and refurbishing of trunk sewerage system, under an integrated action 
plan to clean Yamuna. 
The water quality of river Yamuna upstream of Delhi upto Palla is within 
prescribed standards. However, there has not been much improvement in the 
water quality in the river stretch along Delhi and downstream as the major 
works in Delhi are still to be completed. So far a Central assistance of Rs. 
403.44 crore has been provided under the Yamuna Action Plan and an 
amount of Rs. 458.24 crore (including State's share) has been spent on this 
Action Plan.

667. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT

Authority of India many private and community zoos in Karnataka arc on the 
verge of closure; and

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) According to Sec tion 38(H) of Wildlife (Protection) 
Act, 1972 Central Zoo Authority is required to grant recognition to a zoo 
keeping due regards to the interests of protection and conservation of wildlife

Objectives of Indira Mahila Yojana 
679. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Indira MahilaYojana is under implementation since 1995; 
(b) if so, the basic objectives of the scheme; 
(c) whether any target has been fixed;

yearwise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) Yes, 
Sir. Indira MahilaYojana is under implementation since August, 1995. However, 
it has been recast as Sawayamsidha since February, 2001. 
(b) Indira MahilaYojana (IMY), a scheme for the holistic empowerment 
of women, had the following stated objectives:— 
(i) To ensure convergence of sectoral  services at the local, block and 
district levels, through active in volvement of women and sectoral 
departments. 
(ii) To optimize the utilization of scarce resources in speeding up the process 
of mainstreaming women in development. 
(iii) To create awareness in women through provision of information on 
different developmental programmes and issues of specific concern to 
women, as also on equality of social status, legal rights (like those to 
property and inheritance), constitutional safeguards etc. 
(iv) To initiate a process of awareness generation/education to enable them 
to understand and analyse their problems and find solutions through 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001] 
their collective interaction to match the individual programme benefits 
to their needs. 
(v) To help women become self-reliant and independent by their economic 
empowerment through income generation activities and active 
participation in decision making at various stages. 
The stated objectives of Swayamsidha are as below: 
With the long-term objective being the all-round empowerment of women, 
especially socially and economically, by ensuring their direct access to, and 
control over, resources through a sustained process of mobilization and 
convergence of all the on-going sectoral programmes, the immediate objective 
are as below: 
(i)    Establishment of self-reliant women's Self-Help Groups (SHGs); 
(ii) Creation of confidence and awareness among members of SHGs 
regarding women's status, health, nutrition, education, sanitation and 
hygiene, legal rights, economic upliftment and other social, economic 
and political issues; 
(iii) Strengthening and institutionalizing the savings habit in rural women 
and their control over economic resources; 
(iv)    Improving access of women to micro credit; 
(v)    Involvement of women in local level planning; and 
(vi) Convergence of services of Department of Women and Child 
Development and other Departments. 
(c) Under IMY, no specific target for formation of Self-Help Groups (SHGs) 
was fixed. However, it was envisaged to implement IMY in 200 blocks, with the 
formation of 200 Block Societies (Indira Mahila Block Societies). In actuality, 
IMY was implemented in 238 blocks. 
However, a target of forming 53,100 SHGs has been fixed in Swayamsidha. 
It is envisaged to implement Swayamsidha in 650 blocks, including the 238 
erstwhile IMY Blocks, with the formation of 650 Blocks societies (inclusive of 
those formed under IMY).

recommendations; and 
(d) if so, the details of recommendations decided to be implemented 
together with the recommendations not to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI O. 
RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (d)The Railway Expert Group headed by Dr. Rakesh Mohan has 
submitted an Interim Executive Summary of the report on 17.2.2001. The Major 
recommendations of the Interim Executive Summary are: 
1. Institutional separation of roles into policy, regulatory and management 
functions. This will mean: 
(i) Policy makers are limited for setting policy (and paying for what they ask 
for). The Government of India will be in-charge of setting policy 
direction. 
(ii) Provide operational autonomy and insulate Indian Railways by 
corporatising it into "Indian Railways Corporation" (IRC). It would be 
governed by a reconstituted Indian Railways Executive Board. 
(iii) Set up an Indian Rail Regulatory Authority to regulate IRC's activities 
as a monopoly supplier of rail servic es particularly related to tariff 
setting. 
2. Ex ante acceptance and commitment by the Government and Indian 
Railways that Indian Railways will operate on commercial lines. Non-
commercial activities mandated by the Government will be clearly demonstrated and 
Indian Railways appropriately compensated for such activities. 
3. In view of financial crisis Indian Railways to pursue the strategic High 
Growth pattern for financial recovery. 
4. Provides exemption from taxation—excise, sales tax etc. for the period of 
transition, say 5—7 years.

cargo prior to shipment and declared the wheat consignments fit for human 
consumption and conforming to the quality specifications of the Iraqi order. 
However, on arrival of the consignments at Iraqi ports, the Grain Board of Iraq 
insisted on "nil" tolerance for inorganic foreign matter. 
The Indian delegation that visited Iraq in May, 2001 was informed by 
Iraqi authorities that, according to thei r definition, they do not count sand 
particles under foreign matter. In other words, inorganic matter, which is a part 
and parcel of forcing matter, like sand, stones, pebbles, clay particles, etc., are 
not accepted under this category. The explanation given by them was that only 
organic foreign matter (like chaff, glumes, weed seeds and other edible and 
inedible grains) are taken under this category. This position was not known to 
the exporters. They presumed that, as in the CODEX standards, the 2% foreign 
matter would include upto 0.5% in organic matter. The delegation was further 
informed that the Iraqi flour mills were not having adequate facilities for 
separation of inorganic matter because of the problem of spare parts required 
for maintenance of such machines owing to UN sanctions. The delegation was 
told that the Iraq i authorities had accordingly taken a decision to reject any 
wheat stocks found with inorganic matter like sand, stones, etc. The delegation 
was further informed that Iraq had also rejected the wheat source from various 
other countries on the same grounds. The exporters have been given the freedom 
to identify wheat stocks available in the Central Pool for the purpose of export. 
However, on receipt of reports of rejection of wheat consignments from India, it 
was decided that no further consignment of wheat would be sent to Iraq, unless 
it was cleaned to meet the specification of the Grain Board of Iraq.

Probe into rejection of wheat by Iraq  
475. PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state:  
(a) whether the Indian high delegation, which visited Iraq to probe 
rejection of two wheat shipment, has since given its report; 
(b) if so, what are the findings; and 
(c) what are the reasons that the stringent quality norms for separating 
sands, stones and other inorganic matter has required by Baghdad were not 
followed by the Indian exporters?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER  
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN):   
(a) Yes, Sir.  
 (b) and (c) Iraq has recently rejected four consignments of wheat exported   
by three parties from India. Iraq has rejected the wheat consignment from In dia insisting that the 
cargo should be totally free from inorganic matter, such as, sand, silica, dust and asphalt, and 
also live insects. 
207 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001] 
As per the International CODEX standards, foreign matter in the grain is 
permissible upto 2% out of which 1.5% consists of organic matter, such as, 
chaff, weed seeds, other edible and no n-edible grains, etc. and the balance 
(0.5%) inorganic foreign matter, such as, stones, dust, etc. Quality specifications 
prescribed in the Iraqi contract provided for the presence of foreign matter upto 
2%. There was no further break-up of this 2% into organic and inorganic foreign 
matter. 
The Indian delegation that visited Iraq was, however, informed by Iraqi 
authorities that, according to their definition, they do not count sand particles 
under foreign matter. In other words, inorganic matter, which is a part and parcel 
of foreign matter, like sand, stones, pebbles, clay particles, etc., are not accepted 
under this category. The explanation given by them was that only organic 
foreign matter (like chaff, glumes, weed  seeds and other edible and inedible 
grains) are taken under this category.  This position was not known to the 
exporters. They presumed that, as in the CODEX standards, the 2% foreign 
matter would include upto 0.5% in organic matter. The delegation was further 
informed that the Iraqi flour mills were not having adequate facilities for 
separation of inorganic matter because of the problem of spare parts required 
for maintenance of such machines owing to UN sanctions. The delegation was 
told that the Iraqi authorities had accordingly taken a decision to reject any 
wheat stocks found with inorganic matter like sand, stones, etc. The delegation 
was further informed that Iraq had also rejected the wheat source from various 
other countries on the same grounds. 
The export of wheat has not been directly undertaken by the Food 
Corporation of India. The exporters have been given the freedom to identify 
wheat stocks available in the Central Pool for the purpose of export. However, 
on receipt of reports of rejection of wheat consignments from India, it was 
decided that no further consignment of wheat would be sent to Iraq, unless it 
was cleaned to meet the specifications of the Grain Board of Iraq.

Dress code for Hindus in Afghanistan 
546.     SHRIMATI JAYAPRADA NAHATA: 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: SHRI P. 
PRABHAKAR REDDY: SHRI K. 
RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Taliban regime has issued a decree asking 
Hindus in Afghanistan to identify th emselves by wearing yellow cloth and 
follow shariyat or face prosecution and that Hindus and Muslims cannot live in 
the same house; 
(b) if so. Government's reaction thereto and the steps taken to safeguard 
the religious and social freedom of Hindus in Afghanistan; 
(c) whether the International Human Rights Commission has been 
approached in this regard; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) whether Government would consider to take up the matter with the 
friendly foreign countries for an honourable settlement? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) Government has seen credible reports 
that the Taliban have issued a decree prescribing wearing of distinctive clothing 
and distinguishing symbols by Afghan Hindus and Sikhs. The decree seeks to 
impose new restriction on Afghan Hindus and Sikhs. Afghan Hindu males have 
been debarred from wearing a salwar kamccz or a white turban. They have been 
directed to wear a black cap and put a red tilak as a identification mark. Hindu 
women loo have been asked to drape themselves fully in yellow cloth and wear 
an iron necklace whenever they move out of their homes. All Hindus are also 
required to display a yellow flag on their houses. Muslims and Hindus have 
been debarred from residing in the same house. 
Government has taken a serious view of the Taliban decree. We have 
deplored and condemned the decree, which patently discriminates against 
minorities. 
The Taliban decree is further evidence of the backward and obscurantist 
ideological underpinnings of the group. Taliban attempts to justify such orders 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001] 
on religious grounds are also reprehensible. Taliban's edict justifies the action 
that the international community has taken in imposing sanctions on the Taliban 
through resolutions such as UNSCR-1333. 
Government has also raised the issue of Taliban's decree in its interaction 
with members of the international community, bilaterally as well as in the UN. 
Consequently, there has been widespread condemnation by the international 
community of the Taliban's decree, including from the UN Secretary General, 
European Union and the US. 
The matter will be appropriately taken up by the Government in the 58th 
session of the Commission on Human Rights in March/April, 2002.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

Pakistan during the recent visit of President Pervez Musharraf; 
(b) the details of the areas of disagreements between the two Nations and 
India's position thereon; and 
(c) to what extent the relations with Pakistan on border issue would be 
sorted out? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN HE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) In dia is committed to establishing a 
relationship of peace, friendship and cooperation with Pakistan. Narrow, 
•segmented or unifocal approaches to bilateral relationship do not work. The 
focus must be the totality of the relationship. Both sides must endeavour to 
build trust and confidence, establish mutually beneficial cooperation even while 
they address, and move forward on, all outstanding issues including Jammu and 
Kashmir. At the summit level talks, Prime Minister emphasised the importance 
of pursuing such an approach. He also referred to specific issues, which would 
help the peace process forward. These included the issue of 54 POWs believed 
to be in Pakistani jails, the extradition of known terrorists and criminals who 
have taken refuge in Pakistan, the need to improve the upkeep of religious 
shrines and the treatment of pilgrims, and the enhancement of trade ties for 
mutual benefit. Prime Minister also fo cussed on cross-border terrorism being 
promoted in Jammu and Kashmir and elsewhere in India, and reiterated that 
India has the resolve, stamina and ability of defeat terrorism. 
Pakistan, however, adopts an approach to bilateral relations that is almost 
exclusively fixated on Kashmir. During the summit level talks, President Pervez 
Musharraf emphasized the "centrality" of Jammu and Kashmir in India-Pakistan 
relation and indicated that the process of normalization of India-Pakistan 
relations would not progress unless the "issue of Kashmir" is resolved to 
Pakistan's satisfaction. He also discounted the importance of the Simla 
Agreement and the Lahore Declaration on the grounds that they did not accord 
sufficient "centraility" to the issue of Jammu and Kashmir.

Pakistan is forcibly and illegally occupying a part of the territory of the

all outstanding issues peacefully through direct bilateral discussions.

Abolition of Child Labour 
†579. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of LABOUR be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have fixed a target to abolish 
child labour in the country by the year 2010; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that a programme to impart professional 
training to child labourers for their rehabilitation is being run by Government 
since long and from 1980 to 2000 a sum of Rs. 567 crore were allocated under this 
†Original notice of the question   was received in Hindi.  
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
[27 July, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
head but only Rs. 32 crore could be utilized therefrom; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefore; and 
(d) whether it is not an indicator of Government's indifferent attitude 
towards the child labour? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) Child Labour is a complex socio-economic problem 
which needs sustained efforts over a long period of time. Considering the 
nature and magnitude of the problem, a gradual and sequential approach has 
been adopted for withdrawal of children from work and their rehabilitation. In 
the National Conference on Child Labour held in New Delhi in January 2001, 
it was resolved that all efforts be made for complete, elimination of child labour. 
However, it would be the Government's endeavour to eliminate child labour in 
hazardous occupations by 2005. 
(b) to (d) The Government of India has been implementing two schemes, 
for rehabilitation of Children withdrawn from work, namely the scheme of 
National Child Labour projects (NCLP) and the scheme of Grant-in-aid to 
Voluntary Organisations. The major activity under the NCLP is running special 
schools / centres for rehabilitation of children withdrawn from work through 
non-formal education, vocational training , nutrition, health care, stipend etc. 
Under the Scheme of grant-in-aid, funds are released to Voluntary Organisations, 
on the recommendation of the concerned State Government, for taking up 
action oriented projects for the benefit of children withdrawn from work. 
The Budget provision for the Eighth Five Year Plan period (1992—97) 
was initially Rs. 15 crore and later incr eased to Rs. 100.76 crore. Expenditure 
during the period was Rs. 74.71 crore. The Budget Allocation for the Ninth 
Five Year Plan period is Rs. 249.60 cr ore. As against this, an expenditure of 
Rs. 136 crores has already been incurred. While the level of utilisation of funds 
was low in the initial years of the Ninth Plan, it has improved in the 
subsequent years. Seeing the levels of utilisation of the NCLPs, increased 
allocation for the schemes for the financial year 2000-2001 have been made 
whereby an amount of Rs. 67 crore has been allocated for the child labour 
projects for this financial year.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR 
(SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) The modernisation programme involves re-engineering of the 
existing work process, re-tooling of the accounting systems and setting up of an 
information technology / computer enabled system through networking of all 
Offices of EPFO. The modernisation programme envisages providing all services 
to every member from any EPF location on a real-time basis and to reduce the

exercise of allotment of Nationally Unique Identification Number is complete.

only to one office where he is registered.

(a) whether it is a fact that dismantling of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) has

(b) whether a study group on development of small scale enterprises

reaction thereto?

INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI -
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) Government is constantly monitoring the impact of the 
removal of Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) and WTO Agreements on the economy 
including the small scale industries (SSIs) in the country. While the removal of QRs 
have exposed the SSIs to greater competition, there has not 
322

been any surge in imports as a conseq uence of this step. A comprehensive 
policy package for the development of SSIs has been announced on 30th 
August, 2000. The policy package will enhance the competitiveness of SSIs 
through easier access to cred it, availability of collate ral free composite loan 
upto Rs. 25 lakhs, capital subsidy for technology upgradation and improved 
infrastructure. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The findings in the Report state that a number of problems that include 
inadequate credit flow from banks and financial institutions, inadequate 
infrastructure facilities, low quality standards of products, use of obsolete 
technology, plant, mach inery and equipment, inefficient management 
techniques, etc. are inhabiting the sect or. Based on the findings the major 
recommendations include a three tier definition for small enterprises, a 
comprehensive law for the sector including simplification of procedure, 
continuation of reservation, selective enhancement of investment limit, creation 
of corpus for infrastructural development and incubation centres, imporving 
flow of credit, through raising limit of composite loans, various financial and 
fiscal measures such as raising excise exemption limit and other measures, 
schemes for technology upgradation, marketing etc. A number of the 
recommendations of the Study Group have since been implemented through 
comprehensive policy package for the SSI Sector announced on 30th August, 
2000.

Contribution of SSI Sector 
616. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the impact and contribution of SSI sector in regard to export, industrial

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE

VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) to (d) the small scale sector has emerged as a dynamic 
and vibrant sector of the Indian econo my. The sector contributes 39% in the

Promotion of Small-Scale Enterprises 
617. DR. KARAN SINGH : Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a study-group of Planning commission on development of 
Small Scale Enterprises have suggested a single unified Act Governing the 
promotion and development of this Sector; 
(b) if so, the drawbacks pointed out by the study group in the existing 
laws Governing Small Scale Industry Sector and the major improvements sought 
to be effected through the new law; and 
(c) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRIMATI 
VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. According to the Study Group, existing 
laws affecting small scale industries (SSIs) could be classified in three categories 
(a) Laws governing setting up of industries (b) Laws governing working of the 
industry and (c) Laws relating to Labour & their welfare. Of these, the Study 
Group has observed that the laws relating to labour and welfare are more deterrent 
and trouble some because small entrepreneurs are not able to comply with the 
requirements of maintaining a large number of registers, forms, returns etc. Further, 
the labour strength of the small enterprises may vary as per availability of orders, 
which increase difficulties of small enterprises to comply with the labour laws. A 
Single Unified Act would cover all aspects relating to regulation and growth of 
small enterprises doing away with the plethora of laws and rules and regulations 
governing the sector. 
(c) Government have entrusted a study for simplification of laws, rules, 
procedures affecting the small scale industries sector to an independent agency. 
They have also been entrusted the task of suggesting a single comprehensive , 
law for SSIs.

618. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that cost and time over-runs of the various public 
sector projects are likely to impose an additional burden of Rs. 40,000 crores; 
327 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001 ] 
(b) if so, the details of the projects and the break-up of the over-runs, 
State-wise; 
(c) what steps have been taken so far to arrest the cost escalation and to 
ensure timely completion of these projects; and 
(d) what further measures are being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI ARUN 
SHOURIE): (a) and (b) out of 466 projects, presently, on the monitor of 
Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation, 213 projects have cost 
overrun and 174 projects have time overrun. With respect to the original 
approved cost, cost overrun of all the 466 projects is Rs. 44,385.4 crore, i.e. 
36%. The cost of a project is approved at a fixed cost at prices prevailing in 
that year. The cost increase due to price escalation/general inflation cannot be 
avoided. The escalation is capitalised and forms part of the cost of the 
project. Therefore, increase in cost due to escalations is not an additional 
burden, but is built in the expenditure planning on yearly basis. The details of 
the projects and the break-up of the overr uns. State-wise, can be seen in the 
enclosed Statement (See below) 
(c) and (d) The steps taken to arrest the cost escalations and to ensure 
timely completion of these projects arc as follows: 
 (i)   review of projects on monthly as well as quarterly basis by the 
Government. 
 (ii)   indepth critical review of the progress by the Project Authorities and the 
administrative Ministries and follow up with the State Governments 
(for acquisition of land and provision of infrastructure facilities like    
water and power, ensuring law & order at project sites, etc.) consultants 
and other concerned agencies to minimise delays; 
    (iii)   setting up of an Empowered Committee in the concerned          
administrative Ministries for resolution of problems; 
(iv)   inter-ministerial coordination for resolving problems of interministerial 
nature; 
(v)   making available matching funds on yearly basis based on updated

cost to complete the projects in the advanced stages of implementation 
along with the revised completion schedule; 
(vi)   reviews by the Ministers-in-charge, the Prime Minister's Office and the 
Cabinet Secretariat; and 
(vii)   In order to bring accountability in the execution of projects, Standing 
Committees have been set up in all the concerned Ministries/ 
Departments, for projects costing Rs. 50 crores and above, which have 
reported time & cost overruns. These Committees arc headed by 
Additional Secretary or Joint Secretary of the concerned Ministry with 
representatives from Planning Commission, Department of Expenditure 
and Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation. The Standing 
Committees set up as per the guidelines of the Planning Commission 
issued in August, 1998, have the mandate to go into the details of time 
and cost overrun and to identify the respective responsibility areas and 
to suggest remedial action. The reports of the Standing Committees form 
part of the revised cost estimates of projects which have time and cost 
overruns and the same are submitted, along with the note for consideration 
of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs. Identification of 
agencies/individuals responsible for such time and cost overruns forms 
part of the action taken report of the concerned Ministry/Department on 
the recommendations of the Standing Committee.

Delays in execution of MPLADS 
619. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that works allotted by Members of Parliament 
under the MPLADS for execution sometimes were bogged down by inordinate 
delay due to procedural lapses; and 
(b) whether in view of this Government would issue fresh instructions to 
executing agencies engaged in Rural Water Supply Schemes, Panchayati Raj 
Department, Public Works Department, Education Department, Public Health 
Department etc., to ensure timely implementation of the schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI ARUN 
SHOURIE): (a) Some complaints from the Members of Parliament have been 
received regarding slow pace of implementation of MPLADS work. 
(b) The Government has taken a number of steps to expedite the pace of 
progress under the Scheme. District Heads have been advised to process and 
sanction works recommended by Members of Parliament to the extent of their 
yearly entitlement of funds and to stipulate time limit in the work order for the 
implementing agencies to complete the given work in a specific time frame, 
depending upon the nature of the work. All the state Governments have been 
advised to issue instructions to all District Heads to quickly process the works 
recommended by Members of Parlia ment and accord administrative and 
financial sanction within 45 days and to scrupulously follow the monitoring 
provisions by all concerned. Meetings are being held by Minister of state 
(Statistics and Programme Implementation) in States to review the progress of 
works under MPLADS. In the past such Review meetings were held in Bihar, 
Orissa, West Bengal, Goa and Maharashtra. 
Enhancement in MPLADS Fund 
620 SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state whether Government arc considering to increase the MPLADS 
fund for each MP from two crores to five crores as the fund for MLAs of Delhi and 
Orissa have been increased to two crores and one crore, respectively? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRIARUN SHOURIE): 
No Sir. Payment of interest alone on past debts eats up 70 per cent of the total tax 
revenue of the Central Government. Payment of interest plus repayment of past 
debt already exceeds the total tax revenue of the Central Government. In this 
background, increase of MPLADS funds is not feasible.

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI) : 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, I rise to move: 
"That this House approves the Proclamation issued by the 
President on the 2 nd June, 2001 under article 356 of the 
Constitution in relation to the State of Manipur." 
Sir, if I recall right, in the last three-and-a-half years of this 
Government, this is the second occasion when I have risen in this House to 
move a Motion of this kind. The first time was in relation to Goa; and, now, 
this is in relation to Manipur. In the other House, there were three occasions 
when such a Motion was moved. The third Motion relating to Bihar was 
passed by the other House, but was later revoked by the .Government, and, 
therefore, it was not brought here. This particular provision of the 
Constitution, that is, article 356, is a kind of sequel to article 355. Articte 355 
imposes a duty on the Union Government to ensure that the Government of a 
State is carried on in accordance with th e Constitution. If a Government is not 
being carried on in accordan ce with the Constitution, article 356 arms it with 
the requisite powers to see that appropri ate action is taken, and Parliament is 
able to ensure that the Government of  the State is carried on in accordance 
with the Constitution. This is one jof the most important provisions which 
bears upon the Centre-State relations. In fact, when it was first adopted in the 
Constituent Assembly, many pointed out that in a federal structure, such a 
provision was rare. It was almost nonexistent. But the Constituent Assembly, 
considering all aspects of the problem, came to the conclusion that, in India, it 
was necessary, though it should  be used  sparingly.     In  1983,  the then  
Prime Minister,  Shrimati 
340 

[27 July, 2001]                               RAJYA SABHA 
Gandhi, set up a Commission to undertake a comprehensive study of Centre-
State relations. The Commission is  known as the Sa rkaria Commission 
because, a retired judge of the Supreme Court, Justice Sarkaria, was asked to 
head it. I regard that Commission's report as a very valuable document for 
studying Centre-State relations and their development in India. In this 
particular document, Justice Sarkaria ha s said, "Article 356 should be used 
very sparingly in extreme cases as a meas ure of last resort when all available 
alternatives fail to prevent or rectify a breakdown of constitutional machinery 
in a State." Then, it goes on to analyse what can constitute a breakdown of 
constitutional machinery, and says, "A failure of constitutional machinery 
may occur in a number of ways. Factors that contribute to such a situation are 
diverse and imponderable. It is, therefore, difficult to give an exhaustive, 
catalogue of all situations which would fall within the speak of the phrase 'the 
Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the 
provisions of the Constitution'. 
Even so, some instances of what constitutes and what does not 
constitute a constitutional failure within the contemplation of this article, may 
be grouped and discussed under the following heads. And it goes on to 
elaborate what is constitutional failure and what is not; these are the cases 
where, if you invoke article  356, it will be considered  as an abuse; these are 
the cases where invocation of article 356 would be justified. The first head is 
'political crisis'. Under this head, it says, I again quote: "A constitutional 
breakdown may be the outcome of a political crisis or a deadlock. This may 
occur where the Ministry resigns or is dismissed on loss of its majority 
support in the Assembly and no alternative Government commanding the 
confidence of the Assembly can be formed." I hold that the motion that I have 
brought to this House today relates to a situation which comes precisely 
within the definition of Sarkaria Commission and it is a kind of a textbook 
case, justifying imposition of President' s Rule. It is hardly a matter of 
controversy. I have not known of a single case during the last 50 years where 
every party in the Assembly, almost  every Member of the House has 
recommended President's Rule; otherw ise, the normal response of any 
legislator is "why should you cut short our tenure; we have been elected for 
five years and, therefore, we should be allowed to continue for five years." 
Whereas, in this case, the last Government, I am not going through the entire 
history that is, the Assembly was constituted on 1stI March, 2000. Since then, 
all the Governments that were formed were unstable. The last Government 
was formed on 15th of February, 2001. It was a Government having the 
support of 59 Members, in a House of 60.   I give credit to the 
341 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2001] 
principal opposition in this House that the only Member of that party 
preferred to stay in the Opposition rather than become a Minister himself. I 
have always had respect for that single  Member of yours in the Assembly. In 
the House of 60, there was a governmental group. It was a mixed group of 59. 
And, out of 59, 34 Members were in the Council of Ministers. So, it was a 
very peculiar case. A Confidence Motion was moved in the House because 
some Members had withdrawn support to the then Chief Minister, saying they 
were not supporting him. The session was called, especially, to prove the 
majority of the Government. On the 21 st of May, 2001, the Vote of 
Confidence moved by the Chief Minister was defeated, with 17 MLAs voting

office till alternative arrangem ents were made. From 21 st May to 31st May-, 
that is, for 10 days- the Governor went through the motion of inviting 
everyone possible. "Can you form th e Government?" "Can you form the 
Government?" And, he mentioned this to all the Members, all the party 
leaders, all the parties, who met him during that period, and, by 31st , he had 
decided what to do. Sir, I quote from paragraph 9 of the Governor's Report 
which has already been given to the Members of the House. 
It says: "I have waited patiently all these days since the 21st May and 
given ample time to all the political groups to come up with a credible

it saddens me to come to the conclusion that the constitutional machinery in

major political parties, I am constrained to recommend President's Rule under 
Article 356 of the Constitution of India." 
This is the Governor's report, which has been circulated, in which, in 
the preceding paragraphs before the said paragraph, he mentioned all the 
names of the parties, MLAs and the party leaders who met the Governor and

Governor himself recommended, "Keep the Assembly in suspended 
animation on the ground that the situation was not yet ripe for holding of

and 18 June saw large-scale violence throughout the State of Manipur. The 
violence reflected an anguished psyche  where people were disturbed by the 
politics of their leaders and, therefore, in the violence they did not spare the

simmering during the last few years.  The incidents which Shri Pranab

how . 'the underground' there was ruling the State. This was concluded by 
everybody in the Government and outside. We know how trucks were stopped

over. There was a Patwa issued by the 'underground': The Hindi telecast in the 
whole region was stopped not by Doordarshan but by the cable operators. 
Nobody could have the Hindi telecast in his house. On every salary day, there 
were deductions from the salary at the of ficial counters in the Secretariat, in 
banks and those deductions were dutifully handed over to the underground. 
The State was in debt. There was no m oney. University teaciers were not 
getting their salaries for months. In such circumstances, grievances took a back 
seat and people started thinking that the people of Manipur are patriotic, have a 
tradition of 5,000 years, are part of the milieu of this country, are part of the 
culture of this country and, therefore, they

are good and, therefore, they are neglected. If you take up arms, if you go 
underground, if you revolt, everybody looks at you and everybody gives you 
concessions. A university teacher said, "Every other State in our Region, the 
Seven Sisters, has a Central university. But Manipur does not have a 
university because Manipur does not have that kind of cesessionism." That 
was the situation in which politicians prospered in a different way. We found 
that the Assembly was constituted on the 1 st of March, 2000 and even before 
the Members took oath, th e Members belonging to fo ur political parties split 
their parties and the political anarchy continued from March, 2000 up to the 
Proclamation of President's Rule. It is there for everybody to see. We find 
that this situation arises because a defection which is sinful, which is 
immoral, which is anti-democratic has been given a constitutional sanction 
by virtue of the adoption of the Xth Schedule. I find that defections are 
converted into splits with the game of numbers and the split protects the 
person in his seat.   He can get away with his sin. 
This is possible because of the provision of split in the Xth 
Schedule. History tells us that one of the greatest splitters in Indian political 
life was instrumental in providing this exception to the general rule of 
defection being a ground for disqualifi cation, and split is, therefore, given 
constitutional sanction. This is almost a constitutional foundation for a 
constitutional anarchy when you permit unscrupulous politicians to change 
sides for the purpose of power, in the name of an ideological split. I believe, 
this is nothing but a fraud on the Constitution. It is time for us to reconsider 
such provisions of the Constitution. History tells us that a dictatorship was 
established in Germany through the Constitution. History of this country tells 
us that a dictatorship was sought to be established in this country through the 
provisions of the Constitution, and we find that a candidate disqualified from 
contesting an election is ruling a State in view of the provisions of the 
Constitution. Therefore, if such distor tions are possible in the express words 
of the Constitution, then it is time that after 50-years of our Independence 
and of our Republic, this country enters into a serious exercise of reforming 
the Constitution. That exercise has now become necessary because the 
defects of the Constitution have been, in a way, thrown up before us by all 
these instances.

about the interpretation of this article. There, I believe, much is desired to be

on the ground of failure of the Constitutional machinery in the State, but on 
the ground of some abstract  principles somebody says  that the State violated 
Constitution. I believe, the mandate in the Bommai case has to be seriously 
debated to find out the real meaning of article 356. 
Sir, I began by saying that if any situation answers the description in 
article 356, viz. a situation where the Constitutional machinery has failed, it is 
Manipur. Manipur is another small State which is contributing to this 
distortion being highlighted before the people, after Goa. I used to tell my 
friends in Goa that they have greatly contributed to the law governing 
defections, by providing case after case and by providing those cases to the 
Supreme Court to lay down as to where a split occurs and as to when a 
defection is illegal and not contemplated by the Constitution, and the 
formation of the Government is bad. Now, after Goa, another small State has 
given us a graphic picture where, even before the Members took their oath, 
they split their parties. In a House of 60, 34 Members became Ministers. I 
believe, it is high time this House and Parliament consider how such a 
situation is not permitted under the Constitution, whether there can be a 
ceiling on the number of Members becoming Ministers under a particular 
structure, whether every Member of the House can be a member of the 
Government and survive on the basis of that, whether this is permissible, 
whether this ought to be permitted -- under today's Constitution; it is 
permitted -- whether the Constitution needs a change in this regard to bring 
about political decency, political morality, and, above all, a governance which 
is pro-people. 
I believe, the Manipur situation has given rise to all these questions 
in which it is imperative for the political class of this country to respond. I 
believe, the Manipur situation has also made us aware that the use of article 
356 can be done in a manner which is correct. And, article 356 needs to be 
examined, for the purpose of cases where it ought not to be used. 
I, therefore, submit to this House that this is a fit case where the 
Resolution should be supported and passed unanimously. Thank you.

unhappy at the developments that have recently taken place in Manipur. I am 
unhappy over the murder of political morality, over the demoralisation of 
politics and the encouragement given to Aya Ram and Gaya Rams. In one

national interest. The Manipur problem has got so many facets. This 60
